oewn-07499405-n.learner: the feeling you have when you want something you do not have.
examples: Absence had increased her desire of seeing Charlotte again
an event to which she had looked forward with impatient desire

oewn-04952234-n.learner: a tendency in a person to want things.
examples: Human desire has no natural limit.
Her one desire was a home of her own.

oewn-00923043-v.learner: to think that something is the case, or true, or likely.
examples: Elizabeth was far from suspecting that she was herself becoming an object of some interest in the eyes of his friend
I have suspected it some time, but I am now convinced.

oewn-00926844-v.learner: to think that someone is probably guilty of doing something wrong.
examples: The police suspected him of the theft, but they could prove nothing.

connotation.why: treats the person named as probably guilty

oewn-00689827-v.learner: to think that someone or something cannot be trusted, and to have no faith in them.
examples: She suspected his motives from the first and would not take his help.

oewn-02268154-v.learner: to give something to someone in a formal way.
examples: I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly.
the severity of that blame which was last night so liberally bestowed

oewn-02268500-v.learner: to give something to someone as a present.
examples: He bestowed the ring on his youngest daughter.

oewn-02329474-v.learner: to give a thing or a person some quality.
examples: Age bestowed a certain dignity on his plain face.

oewn-05136830-n.learner: how far it is from one place to another place.
examples: The distance is nothing, when one has a motive; only three miles.
It must be very agreeable to her to be settled within so easy a distance of her own family and friends.

oewn-05091408-n.learner: the amount of space that lies between two things or two points.
examples: The distance between the two chairs was only a few feet.

oewn-08573923-n.learner: the part of what you can see that lies far away from you.
examples: A church tower rose out of the trees in the distance.

oewn-01170315-v.learner: to eat your dinner, the main meal of the day.
examples: The Bennets were engaged to dine with the Lucases
She had also asked him twice to dine at Rosings

oewn-01170114-v.learner: to give someone dinner as your guest.
examples: The college dines its visitors in the great hall.

oewn-02965981-n.learner: one of a set of small stiff pieces of paper with marks on them, used for playing games or for telling fortunes.
examples: Do you prefer reading to cards?
when persons sit down to a card table they must take their chance of these things

oewn-06639513-n.learner: a flat four-sided piece of stiff paper that you send to someone with a message on it, sometimes with a printed greeting or picture.
examples: as soon as Nicholls has made white soup enough I shall send round my cards
receiving the invitation from Mr. Bingley himself, instead of a ceremonious card

oewn-06489042-n.learner: a card that shows who the person carrying it is.
examples: The guard would not let her in until she showed her card.

oewn-10208334-n.learner: a servant who is paid to do the work of the house in someone's home.
examples: She longed to inquire of the housekeeper whether her master were really absent
And you saw the old housekeeper, I suppose?

oewn-02293158-v.learner: to win something by your own effort.
examples: Mrs. Bennet, who fancied she had gained a complete victory over him, continued her triumph
She had gained her point, and had time to consider of it.
In a few days more, we may gain some news of them
She wanted to hear of him, when there seemed the least chance of gaining intelligence.

oewn-02295422-v.learner: to get something good out of a thing.
examples: Both sides gained by the agreement.

oewn-07549366-n.learner: a feeling of very deep unhappiness.
examples: Elizabeth, who knew this to be levelled at Mr. Darcy, was in such misery of shame that she could hardly keep her seat.
Elizabeth's misery increased at such unnecessary, such officious attention!

oewn-14471799-n.learner: a bad state of life caused by suffering or bad luck.
examples: The war left whole villages in misery.

oewn-04756076-n.learner: the fact of not being like something else.
examples: But that is one great difference between us.
The five weeks which she had now passed in Kent had made a great difference in the country

oewn-07196595-n.learner: a disagreement or an argument about something that matters.
examples: She then changed the discourse to one more gratifying to each, and on which there could be no difference of sentiment.
